questions.question: Explain the difference between a movement along the demand curve and a shift of the demand curve, and state the one question you ask to tell them apart.
questions.expected_answer: A movement along the curve happens when the good's own price changes — buyers respond to price on the same curve. A shift happens when a non-price factor (income, substitutes, tastes, population) changes buyer behaviour at every price. The test question: did the good's own price cause the change? If yes, move along; if no, shift the whole curve.

questions.question: Why can neither a price above equilibrium nor a price below equilibrium last? Describe the self-correcting process in each case.
questions.expected_answer: Above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, creating a surplus; unsold stock pressures sellers to cut prices, moving price down toward equilibrium. Below equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, creating a shortage; competing buyers bid the price up. Only at equilibrium is there no pressure for change.

questions.question: In your own words, walk through the reasoning for the maize drought question: which curve shifts, why, in which direction, and what happens to equilibrium price and quantity.
questions.expected_answer: The drought hits producers, so it is a supply-side change not caused by the maize price — the whole supply curve shifts, and it shifts left because less can be offered at every price. Demand stays put since income is unchanged. The shortage at the old price bids the price up, so the new equilibrium has a higher price and a smaller quantity traded.
